title: How AES Works: From Block Ciphers to GCM Authentication
description: Learn how AES key sizes, modes, and authentication tags differ, then reproduce CBC encryption, decryption, and the missing-IV error.
content:
AES is a symmetric block cipher. It applies several rounds of reversible transformations to a fixed-size plaintext block using a key. The ciphertext block is the same size, and decryption uses the same key. The mode of operation determines how the cipher handles messages that span multiple blocks and whether it verifies the integrity of the ciphertext. [S1][S2][S3][S4]

Key size and block size

AES transforms 128 bits, or 16 bytes, at a time. The suffixes in AES-128, AES-192, and AES-256 give the key sizes in bits, corresponding to 16, 24, and 32 bytes. A longer key still operates on 16-byte blocks. If a setting specifies AES-256, verify the raw key length and look up the parameters required by the mode separately. [S1]

Distinguish bytes from characters. Encoding a key as Hex produces a longer string. If a program encodes that Hex string as plain text, it gets a different byte sequence. When troubleshooting interoperability, first compare the decoded byte lengths on both sides. Then determine whether the key material is raw random bytes, an encoded key, or a passphrase that still needs key derivation.

How AES transforms a plaintext block

AES loads a block of bytes into its state. Before the rounds begin, it XORs the state with a round key. AES derives the round keys by expanding the original key. The same original key produces the same sequence of round keys, which both sides use to process the block during encryption and decryption. [S3]

A regular round starts with byte substitution (SubBytes). It then shifts the rows (ShiftRows), so bytes from the same column can move to different columns. Next, MixColumns combines bytes within each column so that they jointly affect the output. Finally, AddRoundKey XORs the round key into the state. The final round skips MixColumns. The three key sizes use 10, 12, and 14 rounds, respectively, with the same fixed block size. [S1][S3]

Decryption recovers the data by applying the inverse transformations. This reversibility applies to the block transformation itself. Recovering the entire message also depends on how the receiver extracts the ciphertext and handles the parameters, and on whether the mode requires successful authentication first.

Use a single-block test without padding to isolate the block transformation. Give all three variants the same plaintext block and a test key of the appropriate length for each. Record the ciphertext length and decrypt with the corresponding key. Verify the output length and plaintext recovery separately. The length reflects the AES block size. Testing recovery can reveal a wrong key or a mismatched sample. To verify conformance with the specification, compare the ciphertext with a known test vector. [S1][S3]

How modes apply AES to messages

ECB processes each block independently. Identical plaintext blocks encrypted with the same key produce identical ciphertext blocks. To see this, pass test text made up of repeated full blocks to ECB and compare the output block by block. Matching ciphertext blocks reveal the repeated structure even when the output looks scrambled. [S2]

Before encrypting each block, CBC XORs the current plaintext block with the preceding ciphertext block. The first block uses an initialization vector (IV). CTR uses AES to encrypt counter blocks, then XORs their output with the message bytes. Verify whether the API expects a CBC IV or a CTR counter parameter. Inputs of the same length can serve different purposes. [S2]

Now test CBC with the same plaintext and key. Change only the IV, compare the first ciphertext block, then decrypt with the new IV. The difference between the two encryptions is visible in the first block. Split the ciphertext into blocks before comparing it. Comparing only the first few characters of an encoded string can pick up differences in encoding. This test shows how the mode prepares the input to AES. [S1][S2]

ModeTest setupOutput comparison
ECBUse identical full plaintext blocksVerify that the corresponding ciphertext blocks match
CBCKeep the plaintext and key fixed and change only the IVSee whether the first ciphertext block changes
CTREncrypt the first counter blockXOR the result with the plaintext bytes and compare the output

When padding and ciphertext encoding happen

A CBC API with padding pads the message to a whole number of blocks before encryption and removes the padding after decryption using the same rules. With the default padding, a plaintext of exactly 16 bytes gets an extra block of padding and produces 32 bytes of ciphertext. When switching libraries, use the same padding rules and the same input bytes. [S1][S5]

Hex and Base64 encoding happen after encryption. The same ciphertext bytes can be represented by either kind of string. Decode both to bytes before comparing them. Try a public sample in the Base64 encoder and decoder, then verify whether the encryption API accepts text or bytes. To compute a digest, use the hash calculator. A hash gives you a digest to compare, while AES lets you recover the original data with the key.

When testing an API with Chinese text, padding depends on the encoded byte length. Print that length before encryption, then compare output lengths for different samples with the same byte length. During troubleshooting, record plaintext encoding, padding, and ciphertext encoding as separate fields so the output format and input character set are easy to distinguish.

Why GCM outputs ciphertext and an authentication tag

GCM uses AES on counter blocks to encrypt the message and generates an authentication tag. Both sides can agree on additional authenticated data (AAD), such as a record type that must be transmitted in plaintext. The protocol carries this data separately, and GCM authenticates it. If the receiver supplies different AAD bytes, verification fails even when the ciphertext is intact. [S4][S6]

In the AES-GCM configuration specified by the cited RFC, the nonce is 12 bytes and the tag is 16 bytes. Each encryption with the same key must use a different nonce. For decryption, retrieve the original nonce for that message. Define where the nonce is stored in the record so the receiver can retrieve it for each message. [S6]

When defining a message format, specify which fields make up the AAD and how to order and encode them during serialization. If the sender authenticates the original field bytes, the receiver must use the same representation. Even if both sides parse the same object, reformatting it or reordering its fields changes the bytes used for authentication. Include these differences in interoperability tests to catch problems a plaintext round-trip test can miss. [S4][S6]

Where APIs put the authentication tag

Before passing a GCM message to another library, verify how each API represents the ciphertext and tag. Web Crypto appends the tag to the ciphertext. In Node.js, node:crypto exposes the tag separately through getAuthTag(). Pass it back with setAuthTag() during decryption. [S4][S5]

If the ciphertext and tag are concatenated, split them at the boundary determined by the agreed tag length. Pass both parts to Node.js and use the outcome of final() to determine whether authentication succeeded. If the tag is missing or the ciphertext has changed, the final call throws. Discard any decrypted bytes already read. On authentication failure, Web Crypto rejects with OperationError. [S4][S5]

Have the sender record the byte lengths of the ciphertext and tag, and have the receiver record the lengths it actually receives. This helps identify duplicate tags, missing tags, and incorrect split points. To test a modified tag, keep the original ciphertext, key, IV, and AAD so you can isolate the failure to tag verification. [S4][S5]

Try CBC encryption and decryption in the browser

Open the symmetric encryption tool and select AES, CBC, and Hex. Enter a public test passphrase in the key field and AES demo in the plaintext field. Use any 32-character Hex string as the test IV, such as one made entirely of the letter a. Click Encrypt. The output box shows Hex ciphertext and the status indicates that encryption completed. Use the fixed parameters only to rerun the example. [S1][S2]

Paste the ciphertext into the input box. Keep the passphrase, mode, and IV the same, then click Decrypt. The output box shows AES demo again. The tool derives a 256-bit key from the passphrase using a fixed salt, the MD5 hash function, and an iteration count of 1. Passing the same passphrase directly as a raw AES key to another library cannot reproduce this process. [S1]

Tool behavior and limitations

The tool's mode menu omits GCM, and its CBC output contains only ciphertext bytes. Use public data to see how block modes process inputs and what they return. If the delivery format requires authentication, agree on the GCM configuration and how to transmit the tag in the APIs you use. The CBC decryption success status indicates only that the page obtained text it could display. [S2][S4]

If you clear the CBC IV and click Encrypt, the page reports “Encryption failed: This mode requires a hexadecimal IV.”. The field hint says to leave it blank to generate an IV automatically, but the tool requires a value. The output box may still show a result from a previous successful operation. Verify the status of the current operation as well.

When decrypting, the page infers the encoding from the input text. It parses strings made up entirely of hexadecimal characters as Hex and all other strings as Base64. When working with existing ciphertext, have the sender explicitly encode it as Hex and record the encoding alongside the other parameters. This prevents a Base64 string that happens to contain only Hex characters from being misread.

Troubleshooting interoperability

Start with a public sample that encrypts and decrypts successfully, then substitute the parameters from the actual API one at a time. Save the input bytes and returned status after each change to narrow the problem down to encoding, cipher parameters, or authentication.

  • If the key lengths differ, verify that both sides decode Hex keys or both derive keys from the passphrase, as applicable.
  • If the recovered text differs, align the mode, IV, padding, and plaintext encoding, then compare the ciphertext bytes.
  • If GCM authentication fails, verify that the complete original nonce, AAD, and tag for that message are supplied. [S4][S5][S6]

Record the parameters and output fields for a successful sample in your test. Then create a sample that changes only the tag and verify that the receiver withholds plaintext when authentication fails. [S4][S5]

faqs.q: Does a longer AES key mean a larger block?
faqs.a: AES always uses 128-bit blocks. The suffix in the variant name gives the key size in bits. [S1]

faqs.q: Does CBC decryption output verify ciphertext integrity?
faqs.a: CBC provides confidentiality. To verify integrity, use the authentication mechanism specified by the protocol, such as the GCM authentication tag. [S2][S4]
